4.3 — Chase: The Aggro Radius

Patrol is calm. One distance check turns a guard into a hunter — and you have written that distance check before, for the turret. What makes today different is not the maths. It is that the thing on the other end of the measurement is moving, and that the enemy has to stop doing what it was doing in order to come after you.

In this lesson you will be able to answer“how do I make an enemy chase me?”Solo build
Break It Down~10 minSolo build

An enemy that comes for me when I get close. That is the whole feature, and like every feature in this course it is not one problem — it is several standing in a line, one of which you have never solved before.

First, before any code: cut that into parts small enough that you could look each one up on its own.

No parts listed here on purpose. Splitting the problem up is the work of this lesson — write your list before you open the file.

Most of the parts inside this feature are things you have already built somewhere else: a distance check written for a turret, a movement toward a target written for a guard, an animator value driven from a direction, a tuning knob, a null guard. Only one part has no earlier version, and it is the one to slow down on — a direction worked out from two positions, one of which you do not control, recomputed every frame. That is what a well-sequenced course feels like from the inside: the same parts, standing in a new order, with one genuinely new one among them.

The test for a finished split: could you look this part up on its own, right now, in one search? "Make the enemy chase me" cannot be looked up. "Subtract two positions to get a direction" can. If a part is still too big to search for, it is two parts.

Your turn

List the parts of this problem, in the order you would build them.

Write the rule down before you code it: when the enemy is inside its patrol beat and inside the aggro radius at the same time, which behaviour wins? Say what the player sees if you pick the other one.

The Problem: Noticing You ~20 min

Your goal: the enemy should come for you when you get close, and go back to its beat when you leave. That is the whole feature — and this is the test for it. Every line below is something you can watch happen in the editor with the Console open and the Scene view in front of you. You are done when all of them are true at once.

  1. You stand well outside the enemy's radius and it ignores you completely — it walks its beat exactly as it did before this lesson.
  2. You cross the line and it comes for you: it drops the beat and starts closing, smoothly, without waiting for a turn.
  3. You step sideways while it is closing and it steers. Its path curves toward you instead of committing to the spot where it first noticed you.
  4. You walk back out past the line and it gives up and walks a beat again. You can point at which way it heads first, and say why it heads there.
  5. It never stutters and never crabs sideways while it is chasing you.
  6. With no Player in the scene at all, nothing errors and the enemy keeps walking its beat.
  7. The Console prints which mode the enemy is in, and that word flips the instant you cross the line — in both directions.

Now the parts. Seven of them, and six are lessons you have already finished. The radius is 3.1's distance comparison, pointed at the same player the turret was watching. Closing on you is 4.1's movement toward a target, pointed at something you did not place. Facing the way it walks is 4.2's animator value, set by code you have already written. There is no new API in this lesson at all — it is three old lessons standing in a new order, with one part inside it that has never existed before.

  1. Find the player, once, and keep them. A reference held from startup, plus the guard for a scene with no player in it. (3.1)
  2. Measure how far away they are. The distance between two positions, re-asked every frame. (3.1)
  3. Decide that close enough means chase. A comparison against a number a designer can tune from the Inspector. (3.1)
  4. Work out which way to go. A direction derived from two positions, both of which are moving, recomputed every frame. This part is new.
  5. Move along it. Whichever movement call you chose for the patrol. (4.1)
  6. Face the way it goes. The animator value, driven this time by a chase instead of a beat. (4.2)
  7. Stop the beat while the chase runs. One writer to the enemy's position, and a decision about what the beat remembers when the chase ends. (4.1)
Slow down on one part: working out the direction. Every direction you have written so far came from somewhere that was handed to you. In 1.4 it came from the keys you were pressing. In 4.1 it was a sign flip — one fixed axis, chosen once and never reconsidered. In 3.2 you subtracted two positions, but only at the instant of firing, from a muzzle you had placed yourself. This time both ends move: the enemy is walking, you are running, and the direction has to be worked out again from nothing but the two positions, on every frame. That is the genuinely new part of this feature, and it is where the bugs will be.

The one fact I will hand you, so you can spend your attention on the rest: the vector from the enemy to the player is the player's position minus the enemy's, in that order. Swap the operands and you have built something that runs away instead. And that vector has to be given length one before you multiply it by a speed — otherwise the enemy's speed depends on how far away you are, and it crawls the moment it reaches you.

The second decision is not about maths at all. Your Update() method currently patrols unconditionally, and now it has to be able to chase as well — which means two behaviours want the same object. There is no earlier lesson to copy an answer from here, so read the three options and pick one on purpose:

How the two behaviours coexistWhat the code does each frameWhat the player seesThe risk
Chase is an if; patrol is the else Exactly one of the two runs. A clean switch: the moment you cross the line, the enemy turns and comes for you. Nothing holds the answer to "am I chasing?" — so no other part of your code can ask. It also forces you to decide which wins when you are inside the patrol beat and the radius at the same time.
Chase is an if; the patrol keeps running anyway Both write to the enemy's position in the same frame. A stutter, or an enemy that drifts toward you while still dutifully flipping at the end of its beat. Two systems moving one object. Their sum is a third movement that nobody designed — and it is the single most common bug in this lesson.
Chase is an if; the patrol is switched off by a flag The flag records the mode, and the patrol checks it. Same as the first row, at first. One extra field, and one extra thing to keep true. Harmless for two behaviours — and the seed of a real problem once you have four. Keep this thought for 4.5.
The bug you are most likely to write today. If your patrol code still runs while the chase runs, the enemy receives two movement instructions per frame. With the 4.1 leash approach this is especially easy to miss, because the patrol's flip check is still measuring distance from the spawn anchor and happily reversing your chase mid-pursuit. Watch the enemy's motion: a hunter that stutters or crabs sideways is not chasing badly, it is patroling and chasing at once.

Socratic: States, Transitions and Two Writers

  1. You gave the turret a distance check in 3.1 and it opened fire. What does the enemy do with that same answer that the turret did not do — and why does that make the enemy harder to build?
  2. Your enemy is inside its patrol beat and inside the aggro radius at the same time. Which behaviour must win? Describe exactly what the player sees if you pick the other one.
  3. If both behaviours move the transform in one frame, what is the sum of "walk right at 2 units per second" and "walk toward the player at 2 units per second"? Why is that sum not a chase — and which direction does the enemy actually travel?
Build Lab: Turn the Guard Into a Hunter ~30 min

Open Assets/Scripts/EnemyController.cs — the patrol you wrote in 4.1. Everything today is an addition to that file. Save the scene first: you are about to give four enemies an opinion about you.

Architectural specification for the chase:

Acquiring the target:

  • Which of the two targeting options from 3.1 did you choose, and what does that choice cost across four enemy instances?
  • Which lifecycle method holds the lookup so it runs once rather than every frame? What did you do in 3.1, and is the reason the same?
  • What does FindWithTag return when nothing matches, and what guard clause must follow it?
  • Should the guard clause stop the whole update, or only the chase half? What does the enemy need to keep doing when there is no player in the scene?

The aggro knob:

  • What serialized float lets a designer set how close you must get before the enemy turns? What do you name it so a stranger reading the Inspector understands the relationship to the patrol knob beside it?
  • Choose a default and justify it against the size of the Overworld, your patrol beat, and the turret's detection range from 3.1. Which of those two radii should be larger, and what does the player feel if it is the other way round?

The pursuit:

  • Which subtraction order gives you a vector pointing from the enemy to the player? State it, then say what the other order produces.
  • Why must that vector be normalized before you multiply it by a speed? Describe the enemy's approach curve without it — an enemy that slows down as it closes is not a hunter.
  • Which movement call moves the enemy, and is it the same one your patrol uses? If the patrol and the chase use different movement methods, what does the Rigidbody2D have to satisfy for both?
  • Both positions are moving now. Where in the frame does the direction have to be worked out so that the enemy is steering at where you are, rather than at where you were?

The transition — the problem with no earlier lesson to copy:

  • Which of the three coexistence designs did you choose? Write it down before you code it, including what happens at exactly the aggro boundary.
  • What guarantees that only one of the two behaviours moves the enemy in any given frame? Point at the exact construct in your own file.
  • Should the patrol's own memory — its direction and its anchor — be reset or preserved when the chase ends? What does the player see if you preserve it, and what do they see if you reset it?
  • Which animator Direction value should be set while chasing, and how does the enemy's animator cope with a direction that changes every frame? (Re-read your 4.2 notes rather than guessing.)

Proving it:

  • How do you print the current mode to the Console so you can watch the transition happen? What word would you print for each mode?
  • Which of the test lines at the top of this lesson can you tick off with the Console alone, and which ones need the Scene view as well?

When you are stuck, this is the order to reread:

  1. 3.1 — the distance check, the radius, and the comparison at the boundary
  2. 4.1 — your patrol: the beat, the anchor and the direction field it already keeps
  3. 4.2 — the enemy animator, its four Direction values, and why a wrong value is silent
  4. 3.2 — the last time you subtracted two positions to get a direction
  5. 1.5 — vectors and normalizing, where the diagonal bug was fixed
  6. Unity + C# Quick Reference — when you know the name and need the exact spelling

That list is the point of the lesson. When you have forgotten how to normalize a vector, you do not ask a person and you do not guess — you go and read the lesson where you already did it. A working programmer spends most of the day reading, and this list is what "reading the documentation for each part" looks like when the documentation is your own course.

Test the mode before you test the movement. Print the mode, walk across the boundary, and watch the word change before you touch anything else. A hunter that never gives up and a guard that never started look identical when you are standing in the wrong place — the Console is what tells the two apart.

Save and play. Walk toward an enemy from a distance and watch the Console. You should see the mode change the instant you cross the boundary, and change back when you walk away — and while chasing, the enemy's movement should be smooth and single-minded.

Checkpoint — before moving on, you must be able to:

  • Break the chase into parts, and say in one line what each part does
  • Name, for each part, the earlier lesson you already built it in
  • Compare Vector3.Distance against sqrMagnitude, and say which you chose for the enemy and why
  • Compare FindWithTag against a serialized reference, and account for the four enemy instances
  • State which subtraction order produces a pursuit vector, and why normalizing matters
  • Explain your patrol-to-chase transition, and point at the construct that stops both behaviours running at once
  • Explain why two writers on one transform produce motion nobody designed
  • Design an aggro radius that reads as fair next to the turret's range
  • Commit and push
